Photograph: AP Sonya Massey Illinois officer who killed Sonya Massey denied medical release from prison Sean Grayson, diagnosed with colon cancer, was sentenced to 20 years for killing Massey in Springfield in 2024 Associated Press Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former Illinois sheriff’s deputy won’t get an early medical release from his two-decade prison sentence for killing Sonya Massey inside her home after the Black woman called 911 about a possible prowler, state officials decided on Friday. Sean Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer prior to the 2024 shooting, and his attorney noted in January that the cancer had advanced to his liver and lungs. The three-member Illinois prisoner review board voted unanimously on Friday to deny Grayson’s application for early medical release, panel spokesperson Liz Mitchell said in an email. Grayson, who is white, was convicted in October of second-degree murder for Massey’s killing, a case that sparked protests over systemic racism and a US justice department review. View image in fullscreen Bodycam footage shows Sonya Massey and Sean Grayson outside her home in Springfield. Photograph: Illinois state police/AP Body-camera footage showed Grayson and another deputy enter Massey’s home in Springfield, Illinois. Minutes later, Grayson shot the 36-year-old single mother in the face as she moved a pot of hot water from the stove and told him: “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.” Grayson was given 20 years, the maximum possible sentence, in January. He filed for early release from prison in May, six months into his sentence, according to a copy of his application published by Capitol News Illinois. Grayson apologized for Massey’s death at his January sentencing but in the release application wrote she had “attacked me with a pot of boiling water”. Attorney Daniel Fultz, who has represented Grayson, declined to comment. In a letter to the board opposing Grayson’s release, Sangamon county state’s attorney John Milhiser said the former deputy’s medical condition was already considered at sentencing. “To release Grayson under these circumstances would be a miscarriage of justice,” he wrote, “and an insult to Sonya Massey’s memory and family.” Representing Massey’s family, attorneys Ben Crump and Antonio Romanucci said on Friday that the board “made the right decision”. “The board recognized what this family has said from the start,” they said in a statement. “No one is above accountability, and a badge does not provide an early way out.” Democratic governor JB Pritzker said in a statement that Illinois law requires the prisoner review board to consider medical release requests. He called Massey’s killing “a profound loss”. “Sonya was innocent, unarmed, and calling law enforcement for help,” he said. “It was a painful reminder that too many innocent Black Americans have faced this kind of violence – and they deserve justice.” Explore more on these topics Sonya Massey US crime US policing Illinois news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/.text: With the European Cyber Resilience Act's first reporting deadline approaching in September 2026, Cattron is among the first industrial and locomotive remote control manufacturers to confirm that CRA-ready products are available now. WARREN, Ohio , Aug. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cattron , a global leader in radio remote control, engine and generator control panels, and cloud-based monitoring and control solutions, announced that a broad range of its industrial and locomotive wireless remote control and safety products meet the requirements of the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) . The announcement positions Cattron among the first manufacturers in the industrial remote control sector to confirm alignment with CRA cybersecurity expectations, giving OEMs, integrators and end users a clear path to achieve compliance ahead of upcoming regulatory deadlines. Continue Reading The announcement positions Cattron among the first manufacturers in the industrial remote control sector to confirm alignment with CRA cybersecurity expectations, giving OEMs, integrators and end users a clear path to achieve compliance ahead of upcoming regulatory deadlines. The CRA is a European regulation that introduces mandatory cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements sold in the EU market. It requires manufacturers to build cybersecurity into product design, maintain vulnerability management throughout the product lifecycle and provide ongoing security updates and support. The regulation entered into force on Dec. 10, 2024, with manufacturer reporting obligations taking effect Sept. 11, 2026, and full compliance required by Dec. 11, 2027. For industrial and locomotive wireless remote control systems, the implications are significant. "The CRA represents a fundamental shift in how our industry must approach cybersecurity," said Stefan Schwiers, vice president of sales for Cattron's European market. "It is no longer enough to add security features after the fact. Manufacturers must prove a secure lifecycle, from initial design through long-term post-market support. We have been engineering our products around these principles, and we are ready to support customers who need solutions now." Cattron's CRA-ready product portfolio spans its core industrial and locomotive remote control and safety system brands: EC/LO Pro locomotive control systems (model E) Safe-E-Stop and Safe-D-Stop wireless emergency stop systems CattronControl bellybox systems purchased after June 1, 2026, with the CRA-ready option: LRC-M1, LRC-L1, CT24 and MMCU4 (model E) Excalibur-E industrial remote control XBMCU and CBMCU receivers Remtron: 411, 611 and PatriotPro handheld transmitters; 10R, 11R and 17R receivers Tyro remote control systems (based on application) These products incorporate a secure-by-design architecture aligned with the CRA's Annex I requirements, including encrypted wireless communication and other features to prevent unauthorized access. Cattron's newest generation of industrial remote control systems include secure configuration management. The systems are designed to defend against the specific threat scenarios identified by the CRA, and therefore, against unauthorized access at the machine interface. Cattron's compliance approach is guided by the relevant international standards for industrial automation and control system security, which the European Union has broadly mapped to CRA requirements consistent with CRA obligations. Beyond product-level preparedness, Cattron has committed to lifecycle cybersecurity support for its fielded systems. Industrial remote controls are often deployed for 10 to 20 years in harsh or remote environments where conventional network-based patching is impractical. Cattron addresses this reality through controlled hardware and firmware module updates, serial-number-level traceability across its installed base and structured remediation processes that ensure security can be maintained throughout a product's operational life. For existing customers, Cattron will proactively communicate the cybersecurity and compliance status of deployed systems, along with recommended actions where applicable. For new customers, the full range of CRA-ready products and supporting technical resources, including Product Declarations of Conformity, are available through Cattron's dedicated CRA resource page . For more information about Cattron's CRA-ready solutions, visit https://www.cattron.com/security/cyber-resilience-act or contact a Cattron representative at https://www.cattron.com/contact/ . Cattron is a global leader in radio remote control, engine and generator control panels, and cloud-based monitoring solutions. Our trusted brands, including Remtron , DynaGen , CANplus and Tyro , along with our global expertise, allow us to provide a diverse and comprehensive range of control solutions worldwide. When you choose Cattron, you'll experience unprecedented efficiency, productivity, and safety benefits. Whether you're in agriculture, material handling, mining, mobile equipment, or industrial automation, we have advanced control solutions that meet the needs of modern businesses. Cattron has manufacturing locations in Warren, Ohio, and Liberec, Czech Republic, a team of over 300 employees, 11 global offices, and decades of expertise, making Cattron a dependable choice for businesses looking to optimize their operations. https://www.dw.com/en/eu-seeks-arctic-st.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Matn Looking ahead: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders gathered in Finland to discuss the future of the Arctic Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic ," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia's war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention. "There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition." The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest." A changing security environment in the High North The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North. "We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said. The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and … uses its presence for hybrid activities every day." Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials. European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as well Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Confrontation replaces cooperation "From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland. For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe. The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies. Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities. "But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW. The United States as an additional stress factor The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies. "Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland , these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation." Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkilä believes the region is increasingly divided. "In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW. He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights. "Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkilä. Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Climate change is transforming the Arctic At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova. Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners. "Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said. He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change." Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience' At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience. "We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said. Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown. His remarks followed Moscow’s earlier warning that European factories producing arms for Ukraine could be possible military targets. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 1, 2026, 11:15 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied EU Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius holds a press conference on the Defense Readiness roadmap at the EU headquarters in Brussels on Oct. 16, 2025. (Photo by Nicolas TUCAT / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip A Russian strike on a weapons factory in a European NATO country would trigger the alliance’s mutual defense clause, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said. He made the remarks to TVP World on the sidelines of a meeting of the European Parliament’s Security and Defense Committee in Brussels on Thursday, Oct. 1. Only a day earlier, Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned that European factories producing weapons for Ukraine could become military targets. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “I would say if Russia will hit our factories in European territory, that would be Article 5,” Kubilius said. NATO’s Article 5 treats an armed attack against one NATO member as an attack against all, requiring allies to come to the targeted country’s assistance. Twenty-three of the EU’s 27 members are also NATO members. Advertisement Moscow’s threats On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that weapons factories in European countries that produce arms for Ukraine are possible military targets for Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated the threat at the Valdai Discussion Club forum held on Thursday, saying Russia was monitoring European factories supplying Kyiv . “I am not saying that we are going to strike enterprises in the countries supplying weapons to Ukraine, but this is a threat,” Putin said. In August, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin increasingly views Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO itself because alliance members are supplying Kyiv with intelligence and weapons. Other Topics of Interest Ukraine Denies F-16 Crisis Over Maintenance and Parts The Wall Street Journal reported this week that delays in maintenance and a shortage of parts had grounded more than half of Ukraine’s fleet, and all of its US-made aircraft could be affected by the year-end. Comments likely to stir unease within NATO An aide to Kubilius confirmed that the commissioner was referring specifically to an aerial bombardment or missile attack on a factory, Politico reported on Thursday. Nevertheless, Kubilius’ statement is likely to cause unease within NATO, given the sensitivity of discussions around Article 5 and the EU’s on-military role compared with the alliance. “When Kubilius will become secretary general of NATO he might be able to claim what triggers or doesn’t trigger Article 5,” a NATO diplomat told the outlet. Advertisement Suspicious incidents at arms factories Kubilius’ warnings come amid a growing number of incidents at arms factories across Europe, some of which have been attributed to Russia. On Sept. 29, Estonia said Russian intelligence services ordered an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics , a Tallinn-based defense company whose unmanned ground vehicles are used by Ukrainian Defense Forces. However, the Kremlin rejected the accusation – as it did after an explosive-laden drone was found at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport in August and following other suspected Russian drone and sabotage incidents in Europe. According to Politico, Poland, Slovakia and other countries are also investigating similar incidents. Rising tensions with NATO The exchange follows months of escalation between the Kremlin and Europe. On Monday, Sept. 28, Russia’s embassy in Belgium said it had delivered a position to NATO’s International Secretariat and Belgium’s Foreign Ministry warning that Moscow was ready to deploy its entire arsenal if alliance members tried to isolate the Kaliningrad exclave . The embassy also accused NATO of an aggressive policy, without specifying which actions had prompted the warning. NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said the alliance had replied to the informal document, condemning Moscow’s “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” and reiterating that NATO is exclusively a defensive alliance. Advertisement Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened that Lithuania would disappear from the map if it lifted its ban on nuclear weapons on Sept. 11, claiming that NATO would not invoke Article 5 as that would lead to a “global catastrophe.” Separately on Sept. 25, Putin repeated unfounded claims about the mistreatment of Russian-speaking minorities in the Baltic states, the same argument the Kremlin used to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Meanwhile, NATO officials increasingly warn that Moscow’s nuclear signaling is a part of a broader campaign of hybrid pressure, including sabotage, cyberattacks, electronic interference and drone incursions, aimed at weakening Western support for Ukraine. Several member states have already stopped referring to the attacks as “hybrid,” instead calling them direct attacks. During his final press conference at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that European calls to prepare for a possible war with Russia could become a “self-fulfilling prophecy,” while simultaneously dismissing warnings of a Russian attack on Europe as “nonsense.” Advertisement NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Wednesday that NATO’s combined strength exceeds Russia’s and that he does not take the nuclear threats seriously. During the same summit in Brussels, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev warned that Putin retains a “nuclear trump card” and called for increased diplomatic efforts to reduce the risk of escalation. Kubilius rejected that approach, saying past diplomacy with Moscow had failed and called for a tougher European response to Russia’s hybrid attacks. Photograph: Amr Alfiky/Reuters View image in fullscreen The UAE ambassador to the UN, Lana Nusseibeh, who has entered the race to succeed the current secretary general, António Guterres. Photograph: Amr Alfiky/Reuters United Nations Emirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general race Lana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s record on human rights and Sudan Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.00 GMT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.36 GMT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeed António Guterres as the world body’s secretary general. Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two-state solution and has won the endorsement of the state of Palestine . She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations. Nusseibeh, 48, has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban. A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job. Fears mount that next UN chief will downgrade climate action Read more Nusseibeh, who was educated at Cambridge University, was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, where her father, Zaki, had emigrated after the Arab-Israeli 1967 war made it difficult for him to return to his birthplace, Jerusalem. She is the niece of Sari Nusseibeh, a distinguished Palestinian intellectual and author of a widely admired book on Palestine, Once Upon a Country. She has justified her late – but widely predicted – entry into the race on the grounds that the UN security council appears to be close to deadlock on the six remaining candidates in the race, with no one as yet able to establish a clear lead after six rounds of voting, the latest on 16 October. The latest straw poll – the first in which it was revealed whether any of the five permanent members of the 15-strong UN security council objected to a candidate – ended with Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica holding the lead spot. But Grynspan faced objections from two unidentified permanent security council members, making it harder for her to claim she is a breakaway consensus candidate. She has support from nine security council members and objections from five. Guterres is due to stand down at the end of the year Other candidates include: the Argentine diplomat Rafael Grossi; the UN envoy from Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Olara Otunnu, a distinguished veteran Ugandan diplomat; and Ecuador’s former foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa. Two previously declared candidates have pulled out. In her vision statement, Nusseibeh said: “At the heart of the UN sits a wager: that states will give up a little today to gain a great deal together over time. “States have not stopped needing to partner with one another, but they no longer trust that cooperation will yield sufficient returns. Rebuilding that trust, with faster, more certain, and more realistic results, is the work of the UN.” Brett McGurk, who served in the Biden administration as a top national security adviser, backed Nusseibeh for her work on Gaza . “How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to UN data? Because of Lana Nussaibeh – a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them … she would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said. Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in Gaza Read more Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who heads Donald Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace, said Nusseibeh “has always understood that the UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build”. He added: “In the Security Council [as UAE representative] she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN secretariat.” But there is a fierce backlash from human rights activists who point to the UAE’s domestic human rights record and its alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan, the group responsible for killing thousands, including in the capture of El Fasher in October last year. A January 2024 report by the UN panel of experts described allegations from sources in Chad and Darfur – including those of arms being smuggled into the RSF from the UAE – as credible. One of the strongest attacks on Nusseibeh’s candidacy has been mounted by Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, over her denials of UAE provision of any “military, logistical, financial or political support to any faction in Sudan”. The UAE says it supports the formation of a civilian-led government in Sudan.
